title: Poetry is philosophy
subtitle: How Dickinson’s poems reveal the depths of the self
author: Magdalena Ostas
introduction: Plato wanted to ban poetry because of its distance from truth. To this day, many philosophers favour straightforward, literal language which they think represents a singular truth. But, by embracing and playing with language’s ambiguity, argues Magdalena Ostas, poetry recognises and evokes reality’s inexhaustibility. This makes poetry a powerful way of doing philosophy – as Emily Dickinson’s poetic-philosophical investigation into the nature of the self demonstrates.
body:
We usually don’t think of poetry as a powerful tool for thinking. We definitely don’t think of poetry as an agent of forceful philosophical thought. We often assume that the arid or straight language philosophers are apt to use, strangely, brings us closer to touching the truth of things. Philosophy and poetry, in fact, have an anxious history whose uneasiness begins with the ancient quarrel in Plato’s Republic, the dialogue wherein Plato bans the poets entirely from participating in his ideal state on account of their distance from the truth.

We so often evince the same fear of poetry when we measure it against the imagined powers we ascribe to philosophy: the understanding and representation of truth itself.

To be sure, Plato’s stringent stance on the poets appears strange and outdated to us today. Yet we so often evince the same fear of poetry when we measure it against the imagined powers we ascribe to philosophy: the understanding and representation of truth itself. For in our eyes, poetry is essentially inadequate to such representation. It may very well present us with beautiful and interesting things, but we feel that it is at heart irrational, insubstantial, and merely ornamental—ultimately flimsy. Poetry’s force is seemingly weak compared to the robustness and solidity of the ideas that philosophy appears to hold out. Philosophers supposedly argue and know; poets dwell, suggest, and describe. Philosophers deal in truth and ideas, and they purport to communicate them in language with analysis and argument. Poets’ currency is images, figures, and tropes. And what good are these as tools for thinking?

SUGGESTED READING Distortion as a path to reality By Ben Ware

Yet there is a crucial counterpoint to these deep prejudices about the value of poetic expression and poetic language. For poetry offers us something irreplaceable from a philosophical point of view: pictures of ourselves, reflections of who we are. Poetic language renders the life of the self visible and perceptible. And this is neither a vague nor a mystical claim. Poets help us see who we are and what we are with a unique vividness and force: what we value, what matters to us, how we see, how we are. They give us evidence of who we are.

Unlike the poets, philosophers aim to touch the singular truth with their words. Poets do something different: they embrace the ambiguity

Poets help us imagine what it means to be a self just as philosophical theories of persons offer us second-order conjectures about selfhood and identity. Such philosophical theories use the same tool as the poets—that is, language—to communicate with us, but unlike the poets, philosophers aim to touch the singular truth with their words. Poets do something different: they embrace the ambiguity—and therefore the power—of their medium. And no poet is as committed to the power of vivid self-description as Emily Dickinson. Dickinson’s craft so often turns on giving us insightful and unexpected pictures of ourselves, especially of what we might call the space inside us. Looking within gives Dickinson an inexhaustible subject for poetry.

Dickinson’s images for the self are numerous and often unexpected. And the pictures she offers don’t always align, which is to say that each poem is a new invitation.

It is one thing to use language to wonder aloud—as philosophers do—about who we are. It is another to witness Dickinson reach for concrete images that can aptly capture our interior spaces and inward lives, as though laying down possible conceptual paths we might follow along with her. It is one of the marks of her poetic achievement that she again and again turns her poetic attention inward, concerning herself with herself, neverendingly tracing and sketching the contours of an interiority that is never fully expended. Yet it is not a spiritual, confessional, or mystical fascination with the self that drives this form of inward poetic attentiveness. Rather, the interest in the self for Dickinson is always impersonal, microscopic, curious, and deliberative—or, we might even say, something like philosophical. In Dickinson’s verse the drive to understand ourselves is motivated by the same questions that drive many philosophical inquiries into selfhood: How do we catch glimpses of who we are? How do we find evidence of our own constitution? How can language help us to perceive and encounter ourselves?

Dickinson’s images for the self are numerous and often unexpected. And the pictures she offers don’t always align, which is to say that each poem is a new invitation. She asks us to trace and retrace “yawning Consciousness” (poem number 1325) as she looks inside and continually seeks to understand her own constitution. Sometimes the self in her poems is “an Inner” from which “an Outer” derives a “Magnitude” (450)—that is, an interiority that lends meaning to an outside world. In a different context, she claims that her speaker is altogether “afraid to own a Soul” (1050). At other times, the self appears as a fully inward self-haunted “Chamber” with “Corridors” in which she encounters an “External Ghost” (407). Yet in other moments, her speaker appears literally to straddle life and death as she confronts the “Fly buzz” (591) around her body. And in a famous moment, Dickinson tells us with palpable delight that she is in fact “Nobody” at all, pointedly turning her driving question around to face us: “Who are you?” (260).

SUGGESTED VIEWING Truth and poetry With Andrew Motion

We can learn a lot from what I would like to call Dickinson’s poetic thinking if we follow the development of a concrete image. “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain” (340), for example, unfolds as an extended analogy between a funeral and an internal state of maddening despair. We don’t need to go too much further than the poem’s opening line to understand that Dickinson traces out here what it feels like to have a breakdown, that she brings this very experience into view for us. The funeral is figurative—that is, it is in the mind or of the mind.

What an image: it signals the ending for the speaker of regular sensations, feelings, and thoughts. To feel a funeral in your brain is to experience the expiration of the normal faculties, what Dickinson’s speaker describes in conclusion when she says that she “Finished knowing” altogether—an alarming state. The poem’s imagery helps us progressively to imagine the condition of ever-deepening inner breakdown: the sensation of beating within the mind, the feeling of numbness, the predicament of full solitude, and, finally, the feeling of falling as though through space. In these ways, “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain” does more than give us an idea about madness or despair. Through an elaborate and strikingly apt analogy, the poem asks us to consider the interior shape of madness or despair. We see ourselves—or our possible selves—when we read Dickinson’s poem. One might say that her language acts as a self-descriptive record, a unique form of evidence.

Do poems contain truths? Do philosophical theories? What does poetry have the power to reveal? What good are images and figures as tools for thinking? Doesn’t philosophy deal in the same language as poetry? Philosophical theories of the self can tell us that sometimes we experience madness or despair. They can give us a second-order account of psychosis or depression, or an idea about neurons misfiring, or a theory about how to feel better. In all these cases, the philosopher reaches with language toward the truth about the matter. But philosophical theories cannot give us evidence of that madness or despair, cannot think with it. They can neither carry us into the experience nor account for its mattering to us at all as an experience—that is, its experiential weight and consequence.

Dickinson’s poetic craft helps us to think about selves in uncommonly lucid and insightful ways, and her poetry can be read as a mode of philosophy as it evinces a probing, nearly investigative curiosity about the shape of our inner experience. In its quest for ideas about selfhood, philosophy must become more curious about poetry’s contributions to the discussion—and about how poems too think.
